lessons.title: Factor Cyclicality: Why No Factor Works All the Time

body.text: Every factor in this chapter has, at some point, gone years without working. A quant analyst who has only seen a factor's clean, long-run backtest, and never sat through its real-time multi-year drawdown, does not actually understand the factor yet.

children.text: Value, momentum, size, quality, and low volatility have each earned a positive premium measured over many decades. None of them have earned that premium smoothly, in a straight line, every single year. This closing lesson of Chapter 2 is about that gap between the long-run average and the lived, year-to-year experience of running any one of these factors, why it happens, and why the honest answer to 'which factor should I use' is rarely just one.
Factor Drawdowns Are Normal, Not a Bug

A long-run average premium is a statistical summary, not a promise about any given year, or any given five years. Value has gone through multi-year stretches of underperformance against the broader market more than once in its documented history. Momentum, as Chapter 2's earlier lesson covered, is prone to sharp, sudden crashes around market rebounds. Size has weakened for years at a stretch since its own 1981 discovery. Quality and low volatility, while more defensive on average, can meaningfully lag during strong, speculative bull runs when the market is rewarding exactly the riskier, more leveraged, more volatile names these factors are built to avoid. None of this means the factors are broken. It means a factor premium is compensation collected unevenly over time, often paid out in a handful of very good years that make up for several mediocre or poor ones.
The Macro Regime Connection: Why Factors Rotate

Factor performance is not random noise from year to year, it tends to correlate with the broader macroeconomic regime, because each factor's underlying stocks share common characteristics that respond similarly to the same macro forces.

body.caption: How factor performance broadly tends to relate to the macro regime

cells: Rising or normalising interest rates, economic recovery, reflation, cyclical and financial sectors in favour
Prolonged low-rate environments that reward long-duration growth stories over near-term cash flows
Sustained, orderly trending markets, whether up or down
Sharp regime reversals and fast rebounds after a steep sell-off
Early-cycle recoveries, risk-on sentiment, easy monetary policy
Credit stress and risk-off periods, when smaller, less liquid companies are hit hardest
Late-cycle uncertainty, downturns, and risk-off, defensive phases
Strong, speculative, broad-based bull runs that reward riskier, higher-beta names

children.text: Case Study: Value's Lost Decade, and Its Comeback

The clearest global illustration of factor cyclicality is what asset managers now commonly call value's lost decade. For roughly the decade following the 2008 global financial crisis, an unusually prolonged period of ultra-low global interest rates favoured long-duration growth and technology stocks, whose value is weighted heavily towards distant future cash flows, over traditional value stocks in banking, energy, and industrials. Value underperformed growth for long enough, and severely enough, that a meaningful part of the investment community began publicly questioning whether the value premium was dead, right around 2020, before a sharp, rapid reversal began as the post-pandemic recovery, rising inflation, and rising interest rates shifted the macro backdrop firmly back in value's favour.

events.description: The starting point of an extended era of extraordinarily low global interest rates that would persist for years.

events.title: The Long Growth Bull Run
events.description: Ultra-low rates disproportionately benefit long-duration growth and technology stocks; value factor strategies broadly lag over the decade.

events.title: Value's Low Point
events.description: Value underperformance stretches long and deep enough that some commentators publicly question whether the premium still exists.

events.title: The Reflation Rotation
events.description: Post-pandemic recovery, rising inflation, and rising interest rates trigger a sharp, rapid rotation back into value and cyclical stocks globally.

children.text: India saw a broadly similar pattern play out through the 2010s, when a small group of high-quality, high-growth consumer, private-sector banking, and FMCG names, often described in Indian market commentary as 'quality compounders', commanded increasingly rich valuations and drove much of the Nifty's returns, while PSU banks, metals, and other classically cyclical, value-oriented segments of the NSE lagged for an extended stretch. That gap narrowed meaningfully in the years following 2020, as PSU banks, metals, and capex-linked cyclicals saw a broad, multi-year re-rating alongside India's post-pandemic capex and credit cycle, echoing the same rotation seen in global markets, even though the specific sectors and timing naturally differed from the US and European experience.
Why Diversifying Across Factors, Not Just Stocks, Matters

Notice that the same macro forces that hurt value, low rates, a long growth bull run, tend to help momentum and growth-tilted strategies, and the same forces that hurt momentum, a sharp regime reversal, tend to be exactly when quality and low volatility hold up best. Factor returns are not perfectly, or even consistently, correlated with each other, and at times individual factors can move in opposite directions within the same year. This is precisely the same logic behind diversifying across individual stocks, applied one level up, to the factors themselves.

body.text: A portfolio holding only one factor is making an implicit macro call, on interest rates, on the business cycle, on risk appetite, whether or not the investor realises it. Holding several, imperfectly correlated factors together does not guarantee the sum will outperform any single one in its best years, but it substantially reduces the odds of sitting through a lost decade in your entire portfolio at once. Chapter 3 is built around exactly this idea: constructing and combining factors deliberately, rather than betting on one and hoping the macro regime cooperates.

children.text: The Behavioural Trap: Chasing the Factor That Just Worked

Factor cyclicality creates a specific, well-documented behavioural trap, and it is worth naming plainly: investors, retail and institutional alike, tend to pour into whichever factor has performed best over the last several years, right as that factor's regime is most likely to be nearing exhaustion, and abandon whichever factor has performed worst, right as its regime may be closest to turning. Global value's lowest point of investor confidence, right around 2020 after roughly a decade of underperformance, arrived just before its strongest multi-year comeback in a generation. This is the same recency-bias-driven extrapolation from Chapter 1's behavioural camp discussion, playing out at the factor level rather than the individual stock level.

body.text: Be especially cautious of any factor allocation decision driven primarily by the last three to five years of returns. A factor that has just gone through a strong, extended run is, mechanically, closer to a point where mean reversion becomes more likely, not less, and a factor that has just endured a long, painful stretch is not automatically 'broken', it may simply be waiting on a macro regime shift that has not arrived yet.

body.title: The Capitulation Moment
body.scenario: It is early 2020. A value-focused fund on the NSE has underperformed the broader Nifty 50 for eight consecutive years. Investors have been steadily redeeming from it, and several financial media commentators are writing that 'value investing no longer works in the modern market.' The fund's own committee is debating whether to shut the strategy down or fundamentally redesign it to look more like a growth-oriented fund.
body.prompt: Based on the historical pattern described in this lesson, what is the risk in the committee's decision, and what would a factor-cyclicality-aware analyst want to check before recommending the strategy be abandoned?
body.modelAnswer: The risk is capitulating at, or very near, the point of maximum pain, which historically has been closer to the start of a factor's recovery than the confirmation that it is permanently broken, exactly the pattern global value showed shortly after 2020. Before recommending abandonment, an analyst should check whether the underperformance is explained by a specific, identifiable macro regime, prolonged low rates, a long growth-favouring bull run, rather than a structural change in how the market prices cheap versus expensive stocks, and should be skeptical of any decision driven mainly by the last several years of relative returns. Redesigning a value fund into a growth fund right after a historically long value drawdown risks doing so at precisely the wrong moment in the cycle.

body.title: Test Yourself: Matching Factors to Regimes
body.question: Based on the regime table in this lesson, which factor combination would you generally expect to hold up best during a sharp, risk-off market downturn?
options: All factors perform identically in every regime
body.explanation: Quality and low volatility are built specifically around financially sound, defensively-behaved companies, and tend to hold up relatively better during downturns and risk-off phases, while size (especially small caps) and momentum (via sharp reversal risk) tend to be more exposed to exactly this kind of environment.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: The tendency of a factor's premium to be earned unevenly over time, with multi-year stretches of underperformance interspersed with periods of strong outperformance, rather than a smooth, steady payout.
The shift in relative performance between factors as the macroeconomic regime changes, such as value strengthening as interest rates rise and growth strengthening as rates fall.

The commonly used term for value's prolonged underperformance against growth stocks in the decade or so following the 2008 global financial crisis, driven largely by an extended low interest rate environment.
The behavioural tendency to allocate towards whichever factor or strategy has performed best recently, and abandon whichever has performed worst, often at precisely the wrong point in the cycle.

body.text: Historical episodes referenced in this lesson, including value's lost decade globally and the performance of quality compounders versus PSU and cyclical stocks in India, are described in general, directional terms for educational illustration only. They are not a forecast of future factor performance and not a recommendation to allocate towards or away from any specific factor, sector, or security. Always verify specific historical return data directly from primary index or fund sources before relying on it.

points: Every factor covered in this chapter, value, momentum, size, quality, and low volatility, has gone through multi-year stretches of underperformance; this is normal, not evidence the factor is broken

Factor performance broadly correlates with the macro regime: value tends to favour rising rates and reflation, momentum favours sustained trends, size favours early-cycle risk-on periods, and quality and low volatility favour downturns and uncertainty

Value's lost decade, roughly 2008 to 2020, followed by a sharp reflation-driven comeback, is the clearest global illustration of factor cyclicality, with a broadly parallel quality-versus-cyclicals pattern visible in Indian markets over a similar period

Because different factors respond to different macro forces, they are often imperfectly correlated with each other, which is the basis for diversifying across factors rather than committing to just one
Performance chasing, allocating to whichever factor just performed best and abandoning whichever performed worst, tends to happen at precisely the wrong point in the cycle
Chapter 3 moves from understanding individual factors to deliberately constructing and combining them, the practical answer to the cyclicality problem this lesson describes
